question: When do spline-based Kolmogorov-Arnold Network modules improve purely data-driven physical operator learning and particle simulation over multilayer perceptrons, and what accuracy, robustness, extrapolation, and computational tradeoffs accompany them?

key_findings.claim: A shallow KAN-based DeepONet greatly outperforms a one-hidden-layer MLP DeepONet on the tested 1D Burgers operator problem.
key_findings.evidence: With the paper's chosen widths and optimization settings, relative L2 error falls from 23.1% for the shallow MLP to 2.45% for the shallow KAN, and MSE falls from 1.88e-3 to 3.79e-5.

key_findings.claim: Depth largely closes the Burgers gap: the deep MLP has lower MSE while the deep KAN has slightly lower relative L2 error.
key_findings.evidence: The deep MLP and KAN report MSE 2.82e-6 versus 5.95e-6 and relative L2 error 0.89% versus 0.82%, respectively. The result supports different metric rankings rather than categorical KAN dominance.

key_findings.claim: KAN branches improve the tested 1D Darcy operator in clean data, but their advantage shrinks once label noise dominates.
key_findings.evidence: Relative L2 error is 2.89% versus 0.39% for shallow MLP/KAN and 1.26% versus 0.42% for deep variants. At 1%, 5%, and 10% injected noise, both families approach a common noise-limited error floor rather than preserving the clean-data ratio.

key_findings.claim: On the higher-dimensional 2D Darcy problem, MLP DeepONets generalize better despite KANs fitting the training set more closely.
key_findings.evidence: Relative test errors are 20.7% versus 23.2% for shallow MLP/KAN and 19.7% versus 23.3% for deep variants. Lower KAN training loss coupled with worse test performance is interpreted as overfitting in the 961-dimensional, irregular-domain setup.

key_findings.claim: KAN improves in-distribution elasticity accuracy but extrapolates much worse under a tenfold load shift.
key_findings.evidence: In-distribution relative errors favor KAN: 2.93% versus 1.35% shallow and 1.10% versus 0.84% deep. On ten out-of-distribution examples, the ordering reverses: 2.17% versus 3.68% shallow and 0.88% versus 3.51% deep for MLP/KAN.

key_findings.claim: Empirical Lipschitz estimates do not explain the elasticity accuracy or extrapolation differences.
key_findings.evidence: All four deep/shallow MLP and KAN models have similar empirical Lipschitz values near four, yet their in-distribution and tenfold-load errors differ substantially. This diagnostic therefore does not identify the responsible inductive bias.

key_findings.claim: Replacing the MLP processors in a graph-network simulator with KANs improves long-rollout sand prediction but not water prediction.
key_findings.evidence: Sand rollout MSE is 0.0236 for KAN versus 0.0403-0.0505 for the three MLP configurations. On water, KAN obtains 0.126 while the single-layer width-128 MLP obtains 0.0916, although a deeper MLP is worse at 0.142.

key_findings.claim: The KAN graph simulator better preserves the reported sand energy profile and remains stronger under 1% input noise.
key_findings.evidence: Across 25 sand rollouts, the KAN model's kinetic-energy trajectory stays closer to the ground truth than the compared MLP processors. Perturbing inputs with 1% noise also preserves its relative rollout advantage in that domain.

key_findings.claim: The graph-simulator KAN accuracy comes with roughly an order-of-magnitude-plus training-time penalty and a binding memory constraint.
key_findings.evidence: Training 1,000 steps takes 6:03 for KAN versus 0:17-0:21 for MLP processors, about 17-21 times slower. A 40 GB A100 limits the KAN width, so the study cannot perform a broad width or matched-resource sweep.

key_findings.claim: The experiments do not establish architecture-level efficiency because KAN and MLP models are not matched by parameters, FLOPs, runtime, or optimization budget.
key_findings.evidence: Shallow widths are chosen by different heuristics, spline grid size adds trainable basis complexity not reflected by node counts, and model-specific learning rates and training behavior differ. Results are reported without repeated seeds or confidence intervals, so some close rankings may be optimization or sampling noise.

method.core_idea: Swap MLP subnetworks for efficient B-spline KAN modules in DeepONet operator learners and graph-network simulators, then compare shallow/deep behavior across several data-driven physical systems.
method.mechanism: In DeepONet, branch and trunk networks encode input functions and query coordinates before an inner product produces the field value. The KAN variants replace scalar node activations with learned univariate spline functions on edges. In particle simulation, KAN processors replace MLPs inside repeated graph message-passing blocks and autoregressively predict accelerations for rollout.
assumptions: The chosen efficient-KAN spline parameterization and grid size represent the broader KAN design family.
Node-width heuristics yield comparisons informative about architectural quality despite unequal parameters and compute.
One training run per setting is sufficient to rank methods when random-seed uncertainty is not reported.
Synthetic PDE and particle datasets adequately represent practical data-driven physics workloads.
Relative L2 error or rollout MSE captures physically relevant quality, supplemented by limited energy and noise checks.
A fixed ten-message-passing-step GNS is an appropriate common backbone for KAN and MLP processors.

techniques.role: Uses learnable univariate B-spline edge functions with SiLU residual structure as an MLP substitute.
Instantiates branch and/or trunk operator-network components with KAN layers for field prediction.
Separates cases where KAN primarily substitutes for width from cases where ordinary depth closes the gap.
Adds controlled label or input noise to test whether clean-data advantages persist.
Evaluates elasticity models far beyond their training-load range.
Replaces MLP update functions in a ten-step graph-network simulator for sand and water particles.
Compares predicted kinetic-energy trajectories across autoregressive sand rollouts rather than relying only on pointwise MSE.

evaluations.setting: 1D Burgers DeepONet, shallow and deep configurations
evaluations.result: Shallow KAN strongly wins; deep variants are close, with MLP lower MSE and KAN slightly lower relative error
evaluations.baseline: Width-1000 shallow MLP and matched-design deep MLP DeepONets

evaluations.setting: 1D Darcy flow with clean and 1%, 5%, 10% noisy targets
evaluations.result: KAN wins clearly on clean data, but the gap contracts toward a shared noise floor

evaluations.setting: 2D Darcy flow on a 961-dimensional irregular domain
evaluations.metric: Training loss and relative test L2 error
evaluations.result: KAN fits training better but tests worse: 23.2-23.3% versus 19.7-20.7% for MLP

evaluations.metric: Relative L2 error and empirical Lipschitz estimate
evaluations.result: KAN reduces error in both depth regimes while all models have similar estimated Lipschitz values

evaluations.setting: Elasticity under tenfold larger loads, 10 examples
evaluations.result: MLP extrapolates better; deep MLP 0.88% versus deep KAN 3.51%

evaluations.setting: Sand and water GNS rollouts after 2M training steps
evaluations.result: KAN wins on sand at 0.0236 but loses to the best MLP on water, 0.126 versus 0.0916

evaluations.metric: Time per 1,000 training steps and GPU memory
evaluations.result: KAN takes 6:03 versus 0:17-0:21 for MLP and is constrained by 40 GB memory
evaluations.baseline: MLP graph processors on the same hardware

evaluations.setting: Twenty-five sand rollouts plus 1% input noise
evaluations.metric: Kinetic-energy trajectory and noisy rollout error
evaluations.result: KAN remains closer to ground-truth energy and more accurate under the tested perturbation

limitations: Model families are not matched by trainable parameter count, FLOPs, wall-clock budget, activation basis size, or memory footprint.
No random-seed repetitions, uncertainty intervals, or statistical tests are reported for the main operator and simulator comparisons.
Hyperparameter searches and stopping criteria are not sufficiently symmetric to separate architecture from optimization quality.
The B-spline efficient-KAN implementation is only one of many KAN bases; conclusions need not transfer to Fourier, RBF, polynomial, or rational variants.
The 2D Darcy failure and water-simulator loss show that gains are strongly task dependent rather than universal.
The elasticity OOD study contains only ten examples and changes load magnitude along one axis of distribution shift.
Graph-simulator width is capped by GPU memory, limiting capacity scaling and fair Pareto-front comparison.
Energy behavior is assessed on sand only and does not establish conservation, stability, or constraint satisfaction by construction.
All datasets are simulated; sensor noise, geometry shift, boundary-condition shift, sparse observations, and solver discretization mismatch receive little coverage.
failure_modes: Spline edge functions can overfit high-dimensional sparse data even when training loss is low.
Learned splines can extrapolate unpredictably outside their knot-supported training range, as the load-shift result suggests.
Large basis grids and edge-wise functions create prohibitive memory and runtime in message-passing networks.
Noise can dominate approximation error and erase any expressivity advantage.
Autoregressive particle errors can compound differently across material regimes, producing a sand gain that does not transfer to water.
Metric choice can reverse close rankings, as seen for deep Burgers MSE versus relative L2 error.
Without seed control, favorable initialization or data order can be mistaken for a stable architectural benefit.
Similar empirical Lipschitz estimates can conceal local sensitivity, off-manifold instability, and poor far-range extrapolation.
reusable_insights: Evaluate new function approximators as accuracy-cost Pareto fronts matched on parameters, FLOPs, runtime, and memory—not nominal hidden width.
Report shallow and deep baselines because depth can erase an apparent advantage attributed to a novel activation family.
Include at least one high-dimensional case, one extrapolation intervention, and one noise intervention before claiming physics-wide superiority.
For learned simulators, pair rollout error with physically meaningful trajectory statistics, while avoiding claims of conservation unless enforced or rigorously measured.
Treat failure tasks as mechanism clues: 2D Darcy points to dimensionality/overfitting, elasticity to spline extrapolation, and water to regime-dependent dynamics.
Run basis-family and knot/grid ablations because 'KAN' is not a single architecture.
open_questions: Do KANs retain any advantage over B-spline-augmented MLPs under matched parameters, FLOPs, memory, and wall-clock time?
Which task properties—intrinsic dimensionality, smoothness, separability, data density, or spectral content—predict KAN success?
Can regularization, adaptive knot placement, or basis extrapolation constraints fix the 2D Darcy and load-shift failures?
How stable are all reported rankings across seeds, data splits, solver resolutions, and hyperparameter budgets?
Can hybrid processors route only low-dimensional or interpretable interactions through KANs while retaining efficient MLP computation elsewhere?
Do energy-profile improvements persist on water, longer horizons, collision-heavy scenes, and distribution-shifted particle counts?
How do Fourier, Chebyshev, RBF, rational, and spline KAN variants compare on the same data-driven physics suite?

competitive_landscape.title: A comprehensive and FAIR comparison between MLP and KAN representations for differential equations and operator networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Directly compares MLPs with B-spline and orthogonal-polynomial KAN variants on differential-equation and operator-learning tasks with attention to fairness and robustness.
competitive_landscape.difference: It finds standard B-spline KANs generally weak in accuracy and efficiency and highlights seed/order sensitivity; this paper covers more purely data-driven DeepONet depth regimes and particle GNS rollouts but provides less matched-budget and repeated-seed control.

competitive_landscape.title: KAN or MLP: A Fairer Comparison
competitive_landscape.relationship: Benchmarks KAN and MLP models under parameter- and FLOP-aware comparisons and tests whether B-spline bases, rather than KAN connectivity alone, explain gains.
competitive_landscape.difference: It generally favors MLPs outside symbolic tasks and makes comparison fairness the central question; the present physical study reports useful task-level wins and failures, but its unmatched widths and costs cannot establish architectural efficiency.

competitive_landscape.title: DeepOKAN: Deep Operator Network Based on Kolmogorov Arnold Networks for Mechanics Problems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Replaces DeepONet components with RBF-based KANs for mechanics operator learning and reports improved loss and accuracy on several physical problems.
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepOKAN focuses on RBF KAN operator networks in mechanics; this paper uses efficient B-spline KANs, separates shallow from deep behavior, and adds noise, extrapolation, 2D failure, and particle-message-passing evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: KA-GNN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Graph Neural Networks for Molecular Property Prediction
competitive_landscape.relationship: Introduces KAN functions in graph embedding, message passing, and readout modules and benchmarks them broadly on molecular property prediction.
competitive_landscape.difference: KA-GNN studies Fourier-based KANs on static graph properties and reports accuracy/runtime tradeoffs; this paper studies spline KANs in autoregressive physical simulation, where long-horizon sand gains coexist with severe training cost and a water failure.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first broad comparison of MLP and KAN architectures across multiple purely data-driven physical operator problems and the first integration of KAN processors into a graph-network particle simulator.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The suite spans Burgers, 1D and 2D Darcy, elasticity, sand, and water; it includes shallow/deep models, injected noise, a tenfold-load shift, energy trajectories, and training-time measurements.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The broad collection of positive and negative physical cases, especially the GNS study, is useful. It should be treated as an exploratory benchmark rather than proof that KANs are more efficient or generally superior: competing fair-comparison studies already challenge that claim, and unmatched budgets, missing seeds, 2D overfitting, poor extrapolation, water loss, and 17-21x runtime are central results.

reviewer_notes: Read all 30 cached pages, including architecture/training details and every physical case. Four direct primary arXiv competitors were checked on 2026-08-23. The conclusion's broad positive wording was audited against each table: KAN loses the 2D Darcy comparison, loses to the best water GNS baseline, and loses elasticity extrapolation despite several strong in-distribution gains.
